newsitem.title: ITALY: Bossi readies march, poll says 'no' to seccession.
newsitem.headline: Bossi readies march, poll says 'no' to seccession.

text.p: Separatist Umberto Bossi prepared to embark on a journey to northern "independence" on Friday as a new poll confirmed overwhelming public opposition to the break-up of Italy.

Bossi, leader of the Northern League party, was due to begin what he sees as a historic "March to the Sea" along the River Po, the start of three days of "liberation" festivities due to culminate in a proclamation of independence in Venice on Sunday.

He was beginning the journey a day after effecting another of his trademark brash actions, summarily expelling one of the League's most prominent dissidents from the party for opposing his plan to declare a separate "Federal Republic of Padania".
Irene Pivetti, speaker of the lower house of parliament until May, was sent packing because she disagreed with Bossi over northern independence, preferring a federalist Italy.
"Who is Pivetti?," Bossi said of the woman, for years the most recognised League member after him.
Bossi was due to begin his journey along the Po, Italy's longest river, at its source at Pian del Re, a 2,040 metre (6,690 ft) high mountain plateau in the far west of the country.

He says the weekend's events will presage independence for the affluent north within a year despite widespread opposition driven home by Friday's Datamedia poll. It found 85.6 percent of Italians opposed secession with only 7.6 percent in favour.

But the survey, conducted among 1,002 Italians on Thursday, showed strong support for a federal Italy and understanding for the popular discontent that underpins the secessionist campaign by Bossi and his Northern League.

The party has built support on deep frustration with high taxes, bureaucracy and perceived southern corruption and crime. It won 10.6 percent of votes at a general election last April, when Bossi switched from a federalist to a separatist agenda
A narrow majority, 52.9 percent, said they believed a federal Italy was the right way forward and 41.6 percent said they considered northern discontent justified, Datamedia said.

Several anti-seccession rallies are planned throughout Italy, including one by the hard-right National Alliance party in Milan on Sunday. Three porno stars joined the pro-unity charge on Friday, baring all outside parliament in Rome.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi, whose prestige could be hurt if Bossi's events draw big crowds, told reporters he had "more serious things to talk about" on Friday than the League.

"Italy is a united country. The country and the government won't be troubled by political projects which have no roots in the past and no future," he said in Bari, southern Italy, where he opened a major international trade fair.

Despite forecasts of bad weather, the sun was shining on Pian del Re, where, against a backdrop of snowy peaks and mountain torrents, Bossi was due to fill a flask of Venetian glass with water from the Po and take a soil sample.
"Padania" flags -- a white cross on a red background -- fluttered in the crisp mountain breeze.

A flat rock, jutting out over the source of the river that bisects northern Italy, has been prepared for the leader who has likened himself to the 13th century Scottish independence warrior William "Braveheart" Wallace.
A black plaque with the words "Padania-Po-15 09 96" has been placed on a granite slab by the rock platform.
After his appearance, Bossi was due to address a rally farther down the mountain before heading for Turin, where the first parliament of a united Italy sat in 1861, and a fireworks display on the Po.
Graffiti on the road leading up to Pian del Re expressed the locals' divided emotions.
"Italy United," read one slogan painted on the road, with an obscenity scrawled beneath it. Others such as "Down with Bossi" and "League=Hitler" mingled with "Padania=Freedom" slogans.
